questions.question: Caroline, before we get into the big arguments about what this novel is *doing*, I want to start with something simple — when you first read that opening, what made you laugh? Because you've talked about Oliphant having this very specific comedic rhythm. Can you put your finger on it?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to perform the comedy of the prose, ideally quoting a passage — establishes the novel's tone for listeners who haven't read it and sets up the contrast with Hartley and Blackstone's more structural readings

questions.question: Eleanor, you've said that Oliphant makes domination look like hospitality — that the whole trick of the drawing room scene is that the power is invisible because the narrative voice makes it feel natural. Can you show us where exactly that happens in the text? Where does the sentence stop being description and start being Lucilla's mind?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to quote and close-read a specific passage on free indirect discourse — her strongest technical argument, which will likely irritate both Blackstone (too formalist) and Woodcourt (too serious about what's also funny)

questions.question: James, you'd push back on that framing though, wouldn't you? Eleanor's talking about narrative voice and formal technique, but you've argued this drawing room is essentially a political institution — that Lucilla isn't just managing a party, she's running a patronage network. Isn't that a bit much to lay on some furniture arrangements and refreshments?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone into his strongest institutional-power argument while framing it as a challenge — the 'isn't that a bit much' framing should get him to dig in and over-deliver; also sets up direct tension with Hartley over whether form or content carries the political weight

questions.question: Caroline, I want to put something to you that both Eleanor and James are implying in different ways — that the opening is essentially a critique, a satire of women's constrained ambitions. But you've resisted that word. You've said Oliphant is *warmer* than that. Does Oliphant actually admire Lucilla? Is the narrator on her side?
questions.intent: Draw out Woodcourt's most provocative claim — that the novel is affectionate rather than satirical — and force the other two to respond, since Blackstone's reading of corrosive paradox and Hartley's reading of seamless power both require more critical distance than Woodcourt allows

questions.question: James, last question for this section — you said something in our conversation that I keep coming back to: that Lucilla's situation is 'uncomfortably relevant today.' But Caroline would say Lucilla isn't a victim navigating constraints, she's already won. Who's right? Is this a story about a woman trapped by her world, or a woman who's figured it out?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest direct disagreement between Blackstone and Woodcourt — his reading implies structural tragedy, hers implies individual triumph — and let Hartley referee by coming back to how the *form* of the novel refuses to resolve that tension

steering_notes: The three readings here are genuinely triangulated rather than just opposed: Hartley cares about form and voice, Blackstone cares about institutional power structures, Woodcourt cares about character consciousness and comedy. The best moments will come when all three are actually talking about the same passage but seeing completely different things in it. Push for text whenever possible — this segment risks going abstract. If the conversation bogs down in whether Lucilla is 'constrained' or 'free,' redirect to the prose: ask someone to read a sentence aloud and let the text settle the argument, or at least sharpen it.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that narrative voice does the political work directly contradicts Blackstone's claim that the political content is what matters — if the form is the critique, does the institutional reading become redundant? Get Blackstone to respond to Hartley's close reading directly.

Woodcourt's insistence that Lucilla 'doesn't need rescuing' is a direct challenge to Blackstone's framing of the drawing room as compensatory workaround for legal exclusion — she'd say he's imposing a victimhood narrative Oliphant explicitly refuses; this should produce heat.

Hartley and Woodcourt are closer than they realize: both think the novel's meaning is *embedded* in its style rather than separable from it. A moment where they agree against Blackstone's more content-driven reading could be productive — and slightly surprising to all three of them.

segment_name: The Architecture of Social Control: Lucilla's Campaign Dissected

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our pre-chat that really stuck with me — you called Lucilla not a character but a 'narrative function.' Which for a novel's protagonist is a pretty wild claim. Can you walk us into that? What does it actually feel like as a reader to be inside the head of someone who's all mechanism and no interiority?
questions.intent: Open the segment with Hartley's most provocative structural claim — that Oliphant deliberately withholds psychological depth — and set up the disagreement with Woodcourt who wants to see genuine constrained agency in Lucilla

questions.question: Caroline, I want to push on that, because you've been arguing almost the opposite — that Lucilla's logic is not only coherent but actually *right*, and that the discomfort we feel reading her is a kind of recognition rather than moral horror. So which is it — is she a function or is she a person who's just been handed a broken set of tools?
questions.intent: Force direct confrontation between Woodcourt's sympathetic-agency reading and Hartley's architectural-function reading — get them genuinely disagreeing on whether Oliphant's refusal of interiority is tragedy or critique

questions.question: James, you've been pretty quiet so far and I suspect you're about to cause trouble — because your argument is that we're talking about *governance* here, not just a clever woman navigating a drawing room. You said something about marriage prospects, parish relief, actual livelihoods turning on Lucilla's decisions. Can you give us a concrete moment in the text where that real-world weight lands?
questions.intent: Pull Blackstone into the institutional-power argument with a request for a specific textual example — push him toward the passage where Lucilla's social decisions have material consequences, and set up his challenge to both other experts that this isn't about liberation or satire but about complicity

questions.question: Caroline, can you actually read us a sentence — or a short bit — where you think Oliphant's prose rhythm does that thing you described, where the mechanics of the sentence *mirrors* the mechanics of Lucilla's social engineering? Because I want everyone to hear what you're talking about before James tells us it's evidence of something more sinister.
questions.intent: Get a live passage reading that grounds the abstract debate in actual prose — Woodcourt's musical-rhythms argument becomes audible, and Blackstone and Hartley can then respond to the *same text* from opposite directions

questions.question: James, last one and I want a real answer — Caroline says Lucilla is resourceful, Eleanor says she's a structural function, but you've been edging toward something darker: that she's not a victim of the system, she *is* the system. So is there any version of Lucilla Marjoribanks that you find sympathetic, or does Oliphant give us a portrait that's meant to be genuinely uncomfortable without any redemptive reading?
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to either commit fully to the complicity-without-liberation argument or reveal a more ambivalent reading — creates a closing tension between all three experts on whether the novel is indicting Lucilla, pitying her, or using her as a mirror for something larger

steering_notes: This segment has a natural dramatic arc: start with the structural question (what kind of character IS Lucilla), move through the textual evidence in the middle, and end on the moral/political stakes. The Hartley-Woodcourt disagreement over interiority vs. agency is the productive engine — keep returning to it. Blackstone is the wild card who reframes both their arguments as insufficiently political; use him to escalate. Avoid letting anyone settle into purely abstract claims without being asked for a passage. The live reading in Q4 is crucial — it anchors the whole conversation in the actual prose and gives the audience something to hold onto.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that Oliphant 'withholds interiority deliberately' directly contradicts Woodcourt's claim that Lucilla is 'right' and recognizable — push Woodcourt to respond to Hartley's framing before she makes her own case

Blackstone's institutional-power argument reframes both Woodcourt's proto-feminist reading and Hartley's satire-of-masculine-logic reading as underestimating the material stakes — get Woodcourt and Hartley to respond to his governance claim explicitly

Woodcourt's live prose reading should be treated as evidence by all three — Hartley can use it to demonstrate architectural sentence structure, Blackstone can use it to show the bureaucratic efficiency she describes as governance in action

segment_name: A Woman's Wit: Comedy and Constraint in Miss Marjoribanks

questions.question: Caroline, you've said Lucilla's wit is essentially a survival tool in disguise — charm on the outside, agency on the inside. Can you find us a moment in the text where that's nakedly visible? Where she's clearly running rings around someone while appearing to do nothing of the sort?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read aloud a passage showing Lucilla's social dexterity, setting up the core tension between 'charming' and 'calculating' readings

questions.question: James, you heard Caroline describe that as Lucilla thriving — but I know you'd push back on the word 'thriving.' You've called this a genuine tragedy underneath the comedy. Does that passage we just heard make you angry, or does it make you laugh? Because I suspect the answer tells us something important.
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to articulate the tragedy-beneath-comedy argument in direct response to a specific textual moment, provoking disagreement with Woodcourt's more celebratory reading

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in here because you've said something that I think cuts right across what James just argued — you think the constraint isn't just a cage, it's actually the engine. That without the Victorian drawing room and its rules, Lucilla wouldn't be funny at all. Is Oliphant making the same argument in how she writes the sentences — not just what Lucilla does, but how the prose itself moves?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's strongest formal argument about prose rhythm and narrative voice as feminist strategy, and directly set up her disagreement with Blackstone's 'trapped genius' reading

questions.question: James, Eleanor's basically saying Lucilla has mastered the language of her cage so completely she doesn't experience it as a cage. You've said we should be angry on her behalf. Does Oliphant share your anger — or is she on Eleanor's side?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to address whether the novel itself endorses his political reading or whether Oliphant is doing something more ambivalent, creating a three-way tension about authorial intent

questions.question: Caroline, last word on this — both James and Eleanor are making arguments about what Oliphant intended, politically or formally. But you've said the real test is whether it's funny read aloud. So put that to work: is there a line, just one line, that you think settles the question of whether we're meant to laugh with Lucilla or feel the trap closing?
questions.intent: Close the segment with a specific quotation moment that holds all three readings in tension simultaneously, letting the text have the final word

steering_notes: The central fault line is Blackstone versus Hartley — tragedy of exclusion versus virtuosity within form — with Woodcourt somewhere in the middle, grounding both in textual specifics. Keep pushing everyone back to the actual prose when the argument gets too abstract. The most productive moment will be when Blackstone and Hartley have to agree on what the novel does while disagreeing about what it means. Don't let anyone treat 'comedy' as self-explanatory — make them say what they think jokes are for.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'trapped genius' claim directly contradicts Hartley's 'constraint as engine' argument — these need to collide early and explicitly, not just be stated in parallel

Hartley's point about narrative voice being 'conspiratorial' with Lucilla is a potential bridge to Woodcourt's point about prose rhythm — encourage them to build on each other here rather than compete

Woodcourt and Blackstone both want to quote the drawing-room management passages but for opposite reasons — Woodcourt to show power, Blackstone to show exclusion — this is the segment's richest cross-engagement moment
Hartley's claim that 'wit requires constraint' is the sharpest direct rebuttal to Blackstone's political reading and should be staged as such, not buried

segment_name: Society's Shadows: The Cavendish Scandal and Social Rupture

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that's been stuck in my head — that the real scandal in this section isn't what Cavendish actually did, it's that Lucilla has to be a genius just to stay respectable. Can you read us a passage that shows that genius operating in real time? Because I want listeners to *hear* what you mean before we tear it apart.
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read the strategizing passage aloud, establishing the tone and setting up the tension between admiration and unease — primes Hartley and Blackstone to respond from their very different angles

questions.question: Eleanor, you've been itching to respond to something, I can tell. Because your argument is that what Woodcourt is calling Lucilla's 'genius' is actually Oliphant *forcing* her into a corner — that the performance stops being chosen and starts being compelled. Is there a moment in the text where you can actually feel the narrative voice register that shift? Where even the prose gets a bit... tighter?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's strongest technical argument about narrative fragmentation and the shift from chosen to compelled performance — get her to a specific passage showing the narrator's tone changing

questions.question: James, I have to put this to you directly, because both Eleanor and Caroline are essentially reading this as Lucilla's story — her intelligence, her cost, her trap. And you want to say: slow down, this isn't primarily about Lucilla at all, is it? You want to talk about what the *drawing room itself* is doing here — what it's replacing. Make that case.
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to articulate his structural-institutional argument against the character-focused readings, setting up the key three-way disagreement about whether this is personal drama, feminist tragedy, or class machinery

questions.question: But here's what I want to push on, James — you called Lucilla's power 'class-specific' and said most women had neither her financial security nor her position. Does Oliphant know that? Is there a moment in the scandal passages where the text itself acknowledges that what Lucilla can do, another woman in Carlingford simply couldn't? Or is that a blind spot in the novel?
questions.intent: Probe whether Blackstone thinks the novel is critically aware of its class limitations or unconsciously reproducing them — likely to provoke Woodcourt, who sees Lucilla's position as trap not privilege

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to give you the last word on something, because you said something almost provocative in our pre-chat — that the scandal isn't a rupture in the novel's structure, it's the *revelation* of what the structure was always doing. If that's right, then Oliphant has been building a trap from page one and we just didn't see it. Where in these passages does she finally let us see the walls?
questions.intent: Close the segment with Hartley's most ambitious structural claim — that the whole novel's apparent freedom has been a controlled illusion — designed to land as a genuine reframe that pulls together all three arguments

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that should be productive rather than chaotic: Woodcourt reads tragedy and cost, Hartley reads craft and entrapment, Blackstone reads class and institutions. Don't let any one frame dominate too early. The most interesting radio comes when Blackstone's structural argument collides with Woodcourt's emotional one — push for that moment explicitly if it doesn't arise naturally. Keep steering toward specific passages: all three experts have texts they want to read, and the contrast between the passages they choose will do half the work. Watch for Hartley and Woodcourt to partially agree against Blackstone on the question of Lucilla's intelligence and agency — let that alliance form, then introduce Blackstone's class-privilege counter to fracture it.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Lucilla's power is 'class-specific' directly undercuts Woodcourt's framing of Lucilla as a sympathetic everywoman trapped by society — push Woodcourt to respond to this explicitly

Hartley and Woodcourt will likely converge on Lucilla's intelligence and constrained agency, but diverge sharply on whether to *celebrate* or *mourn* it — name that disagreement out loud and make them sit with it

Blackstone's 'drawing room as court' argument and Hartley's 'narrative voice as anatomical instrument' argument are actually complementary but neither has acknowledged the other — prompt them to find the overlap

Woodcourt's point about the prose *music* of suffocation and Hartley's point about sentences getting *tighter* are describing the same effect from different angles — get them to read their chosen passages back to back and see if the room notices

segment_name: Narrative Technique and the Unreliable Observer

questions.question: Caroline, you said reading Lucilla's self-justifications aloud is where you really *feel* the comedy in your bones. Can you do that for us right now — pick a moment where the circular reasoning is at its most absurd — and then tell us: is that comedy coming *from* Oliphant, or is the narrator completely sincere and the joke is on her too?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read aloud and stake out her position on narrator-as-complicit-vs-narrator-as-duped, opening the first fault line with Blackstone and Hartley

questions.question: Eleanor, you used the phrase 'narrator seduced by her own heroine' — which is a lovely image. But Caroline would probably say that's not seduction, that's *affection*, that Oliphant genuinely loves this girl's nerve and competence. Is there a moment in the prose where you can put your finger on the exact spot where admiration tips into something more unsettling? Where the warmth curdles just slightly?
questions.intent: Push Hartley to locate the irony with textual precision, and set up a direct disagreement with Woodcourt about whether the narrator's warmth is affection or something more compromised

questions.question: James, I want to push on something because it's a genuinely provocative idea. You're saying the narrator isn't unreliable at all — she's actually a *perfectly reliable* reporter of how Victorian power justified itself. But if that's true, doesn't that dissolve the whole question of craft? Is Oliphant just a good sociologist, or is she doing something deliberately, consciously artistic with that voice?
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to defend the tension between his historical-structural reading and the question of Oliphant's intentionality, and draw out a direct clash with Hartley's 'deliberate artistry' claim

questions.question: Eleanor, James is essentially saying: stop asking whether Oliphant *meant* the irony, because the ideology was always already doing the work for her. You think that undersells her. Can you point to a specific moment — a parenthetical, a tonal shift, anything — where you'd say: no, that move is *too precise* to be accidental, Oliphant is watching herself write?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to make the strongest possible case for conscious artistry with a specific textual example, creating a focused point of disagreement with Blackstone

questions.question: Caroline, here's the question I keep circling back to: you and Eleanor both want to claim Oliphant invented the unreliable narrator before modernism did — but you mean completely different things by that. Eleanor means formal ironic distance; you mean something more like radical interiority, *feeling* what it's like to live inside a self-deceiving mind. Those are almost opposite achievements. Which is it, and does it matter?
questions.intent: Surface the hidden disagreement between Hartley and Woodcourt, who appear to agree but are actually making contradictory claims about what kind of narrative innovation the novel represents

steering_notes: This segment has a genuinely interesting three-way tension: Hartley argues for conscious ironic artistry, Woodcourt argues for radical interiority and sympathy, Blackstone wants to dissolve the question of intention entirely into historical ideology. The trap to avoid is letting it become an abstract theory debate — keep pushing everyone back to the actual prose. Woodcourt is the most likely to generate good radio because she reads aloud well and has emotional heat; use her to anchor the conversation in the text whenever it floats off. Blackstone's provocation — 'she's perfectly reliable' — is the sharpest reframe and should be introduced early enough that the others have time to really wrestle with it. Watch for the Hartley-Woodcourt disagreement, which is subtle: they sound like they agree (both claim Oliphant pre-invented unreliable narration) but they mean almost opposite things, and surfacing that could be the best moment in the segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Woodcourt and Hartley appear to be allies against Blackstone but are actually in quiet disagreement: Woodcourt's 'radical interiority' reading requires the narrator to be genuinely swept up in Lucilla's consciousness, while Hartley's 'deliberate irony' reading requires the narrator to maintain a knowing distance — these are incompatible, and the moment one of them notices is potentially the best exchange in the segment

Blackstone's claim that 'the narrator is perfectly reliable' directly inverts Hartley's central thesis and should produce strong pushback — but Hartley needs to respond with a specific passage, not a theoretical rebuttal, or Blackstone will win the exchange on energy alone

Woodcourt's pushback prediction about Blackstone ('he'll say Oliphant criticizes from a distance') and Blackstone's pushback prediction about Woodcourt ('she'll emphasize agency without historicizing it') are mirror images — both are right about each other, which means the conversation will go somewhere real if the host steps back and lets them have it directly

segment_name: Tom's Homecoming: Domestic Bonds and Plot Resolution

questions.question: Caroline, you've said you want to read part of this scene aloud—that you can actually *hear* the double consciousness in Oliphant's rhythm when Lucilla sees Tom walk in. Go ahead and do that. What are we listening for?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the passage aloud and set an emotional baseline for the segment—her warmth and attentiveness to prose music will draw out the other two's disagreements more productively if the text is live in the room first

questions.question: James, you've called this 'institutional incorporation, not redemption'—which is a pretty brutal way to describe a family reunion. But is there any moment in this passage where you think Oliphant herself seems tempted by the warmth? Or is she completely cold-eyed about what's actually happening here?
questions.intent: Press Blackstone to either qualify his cynicism or defend it more specifically against the text—this will either sharpen his reading or create an opening for Caroline to push back on what he's missing emotionally

questions.question: Eleanor, you've made this interesting technical claim—that Oliphant's sentences actually get *shorter and flatter* in these scenes, and that's not an accident. Can you show us that? Because if you're right, that changes everything about how we read whether Lucilla is in control here or not.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to demonstrate the prose shift with specific textual evidence, which will force a three-way argument: Caroline hears intimacy in the rhythm, Eleanor hears a formal crisis, Blackstone reads it as social machinery—same sentences, three different ears

questions.question: Here's the thing I want to push on, James—you say Tom has nowhere else to go, that the family is just a safety net for failed men. But doesn't that actually make Lucilla *more* powerful, not less? She's the one running the institution he has to crawl back to. Why isn't that the triumphant reading?
questions.intent: Set up the direct collision between Blackstone's cynicism-about-Lucilla and Eleanor's argument that the return actually exposes the limits of her power—both can't be right, and getting Blackstone to defend his version will draw Eleanor in sharply

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our conversation that's stuck with me—that Lucilla was always 'governing a vacancy' and Tom's return fills it. But Caroline thinks this scene shows genuine growth, genuine attachment. Are those two things actually incompatible? Can you govern a vacancy and still feel something real when it's filled?
questions.intent: Force the most interesting synthesis or conflict of the segment—Eleanor's structural reading versus Caroline's emotional reading—and leave room for Blackstone to come in with his more cynical resolution of the tension

steering_notes: Let Caroline's reading aloud do real work at the top—resist cutting it short even if it runs a minute. The passage being live in the room gives the disagreements something to land on. Watch for the moment when Eleanor and Blackstone are essentially agreeing that Lucilla loses something in this scene but for completely opposite reasons (he thinks she was never really powerful; Eleanor thinks she was powerful precisely because the vacancy existed)—that's the most productive confusion to let breathe. Caroline is the natural moderating voice but don't let her smooth things over too quickly; her emotional reading is a genuine third position, not just a warmer version of the others.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone says Tom is domesticated rather than redeemed; Eleanor says the scene shows Lucilla losing the terms of her own game—both readings are bleak but for opposite reasons about *whose* failure we're watching, and they need to be put in direct conversation

Caroline reads the prose rhythm as communicating intimacy and homecoming; Eleanor reads the same shift toward shorter sentences as a formal enactment of crisis—get them to point at the same lines and explain what they're hearing differently

Blackstone's claim that Lucilla's power depends on social performance directly contradicts Eleanor's claim that it depends on the absence of credible masculine agency—these are compatible but neither has quite acknowledged the other's version yet

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our pre-chat that really stuck with me — that the real horror of this novel isn't Lucilla failing, it's Lucilla succeeding so completely there's no 'her' left to enjoy it. Can you take us to a specific moment in the closing where you feel Oliphant actually shows us that hollowing-out happening? What does the prose do there that a less subtle writer wouldn't do?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read or closely describe a passage showing psychological fragmentation; establish her 'existential cost' reading as the anchor the others must respond to

questions.question: Caroline, you've talked about this almost arch quality in the narrator's voice at the end — this knowing wink. But Eleanor's just described something genuinely bleak. So which is it? Is Oliphant winking at us, or is she doing something much colder than that? Can those two tones actually coexist in the same closing pages?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement between Caroline's tonal/comedic reading and Eleanor's darker existential one; surface whether the novel's irony is sympathetic or devastating

questions.question: James, you've been pretty clear that you don't want to romanticize Lucilla — and I understand the instinct. But both Eleanor and Caroline are describing something that sounds almost tragic: a woman who loses herself. Does your structural argument leave any room for that? Or do you think the tragedy-of-the-self reading is exactly the kind of thing that lets the system off the hook?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone to either absorb or actively resist the psychological readings; test whether his structural critique can account for interiority at all

questions.question: Let's get specific about the ending. Caroline, you mentioned Oliphant's closing reflection on what Lucilla actually achieved versus what she imagined she would — can you read us that passage, or the closest thing to it? Because I want everyone to hear the actual words before we decide what Oliphant is doing with them.
questions.intent: Anchor the conversation in a specific passage; give Eleanor and Blackstone something concrete to agree or disagree with; let the prose speak before the interpretation does

questions.question: James, last one for you — and feel free anyone to jump in. You've called Lucilla's kind of influence a 'permission structure': one woman rises, the structure never gets questioned. But by the end of this novel, does Oliphant herself question the structure? Or does the book, whatever its intentions, end up being as complicit as Lucilla?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to make his strongest claim about the novel's own politics; invite Eleanor and Caroline to defend or complicate Oliphant's authorial position

steering_notes: The natural fault line here is between Blackstone's structural-political reading and Eleanor/Caroline's more interior, psychological ones. Don't let Blackstone monopolize the systemic argument — push him to reckon with what the other two are finding in the prose. Equally, don't let Eleanor and Caroline's readings collapse into each other: Eleanor sees hollowness as tragedy, Caroline sees it through comedy and loneliness — those are genuinely different claims. The passage-reading question (Q4) is the pivot: once we have actual Oliphant prose on the table, all three should feel pressure to account for it rather than their own frameworks. Keep energy conversational — these three clearly want to fight, so let them, but redirect to the text whenever it gets too abstract.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's 'hollow self' thesis vs. Caroline's 'loneliness through perfect control' thesis — these sound similar but have different emotional valences and should be pressed against each other directly

Blackstone's claim that Lucilla's failures are structural vs. Eleanor's claim that they are existential and self-generated — this is the sharpest disagreement in the room and should be surfaced explicitly by Q3

Caroline's 'arch narrator winking' reading sits in direct tension with Eleanor's 'flat prose as fragmentation' reading — both are tonal arguments about the same text and neither has fully grappled with the other

Blackstone's charge of 'complicity' applied to Lucilla should eventually be turned back on Oliphant herself — Caroline and Eleanor both seem to want to defend the novel's sophistication, which sets up a productive three-way on authorial intention vs. textual effect
